property_summary: For every call to setOwner(x) only the admin (the deployer stored in admin) can change owner; the mutant removes the onlyAdmin guard so a non-admin caller can change owner, violating this invariant for some caller/address inputs.

For any caller address A and target address NewOwner, the reference contract allows the admin (deployer) to change owner via setOwner(NewOwner) (call succeeds and owner becomes NewOwner); the mutant wrongly requires msg.sender == owner causing admin calls to revert or leave owner unchanged for some inputs.

For any address newOwner, when the admin (deployer) calls setOwner(newOwner) the reference always updates owner to newOwner (call succeeds and owner() == newOwner); the mutant sometimes prevents the admin from changing owner by requiring msg.sender == owner, causing owner() to remain unchanged or the call to revert for some fuzzed newOwner inputs.

For any address newOwner, when the deployer-admin calls setOwner(newOwner) the call succeeds and afterward owner() == newOwner; the mutant sometimes requires msg.sender == owner and thus either reverts or leaves owner() unchanged for some newOwner values, violating this rule.

For every fuzzed actor A: if A is the current owner, then calling setOwner(X) as A must update owner() to X (reference allows current owner to be set by admin too but guarantees the current owner can set owner only if called by admin; the mutant incorrectly adds a require that msg.sender == owner inside onlyAdmin, which causes calls by the admin (deployer) to revert when the admin is not the current owner — thus the property tests that when the caller equals the current owner the call succeeds and updates owner, a behavior the mutant can break for some inputs).

For any address caller and any address newOwner, if the caller is the contract's current owner then calling setOwner(newOwner) succeeds and leaves owner() equal to newOwner; the mutant (which requires msg.sender == owner inside setOwner) can cause such a call to revert or fail to update owner for some inputs.

The original contract guarantees that only the admin (the address that deployed C) can call setOwner, so owner can only change when msg.sender == deployer; the mutant allowing the current owner to act as admin breaks this by permitting a non-admin owner to change owner after takeover.

Invariant: only the original deployer (admin) can ever change owner via setOwner, so after any call to setOwner by any caller, the owner is equal to the caller only if the caller is the deployer; the mutant allows the current owner to perform setOwner, letting non-deployer owners change owner and thus violating this invariant for some fuzzed addresses.

For every caller x and target newOwner, if setOwner succeeds then the caller must be the original deployer (admin); the mutant allows a call by the current owner (who may not be the deployer) to succeed and thus can change owner when the caller != deployer.

For every arbitrarily chosen caller and newOwner, if calling setOwner(newOwner) succeeds then the caller must equal the original deployer (admin); the mutant lets the current owner (who may not be the deployer) succeed and thus can produce a successful setOwner call where caller != deployer.

Invariant: after any successful setOwner(newOwner) call, the caller must always be the original deployer (admin); the mutant lets the current owner (who may not be the deployer) successfully call setOwner, so there exist inputs where setOwner succeeds but the caller != deployer.

For every caller address, only the deployer/admin (the original msg.sender that constructed C) can change owner via setOwner in the reference; the mutant removes that restriction allowing non-admin callers to change owner, so there exist callers and owner values where owner differs after setOwner.
For every caller who is admin, calling setOwner(...) completes and returns true; the mutant returns false for some admin call, violating this return-value rule.

For every caller address, calling setOwner(...) on the reference contract reverts unless the caller is the admin; the mutant removes that admin check so some non-admin callers can successfully call setOwner, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the admin and any provided _owner address, calling setOwner(_owner) on the correct contract sets owner to exactly the provided _owner; the mutant overwrites owner with tx.origin so for some combinations (when msg.sender != tx.origin) the resulting owner differs.
